WordPress plugin that gives site owners a reliable way to request or schedule browser refreshes for visitors currently viewing their site.

The plugin started in 2017 as my fix for a simple problem with single-page applications: when a new version is deployed, connected browsers may keep running stale client-side code until users manually refresh. Force Refresh closes that gap with one-click site-wide refreshes, scheduled refreshes, targeted page/post refreshes, configurable polling intervals, and role-based permissions.

The plugin has grown into a maintained WordPress.org project with 4,000+ active installations, a custom Vue-powered admin interface, troubleshooting tools, release notes, and an optional static file polling mode for reducing server load on higher-traffic sites.
Force Refresh is an open-source WordPress plugin that gives site owners a reliable way to request or schedule browser refreshes for visitors currently viewing their site.
An open-source WordPress plugin, with 4,000+ active installs, that refreshes visitors' browsers after a site update.

The Bicentennial Scholars and Professors pages were two interactive pages for a pair of new University of Virginia initiatives. Built on Alderman, they served as the primary online presence for the programs' combined $375 million fundraising effort. The programs have since surpassed $1.3 billion in combined impact, including matching funds.

Both pages used Alderman's shared modular components alongside elements built just for them. Animated circles, a field of parallax images, and an odometer tracking fundraising progress gave each page its own personality.

The animated circles and parallelograms were drawn in code rather than with images. Images would have been simpler, but code gave more room to animate and stayed sharp on high-resolution displays. Animations were triggered with the Intersection Observer API instead of scroll listeners bound to the entire document, which made a meaningful difference to performance. Despite the complexity, both pages were built within a week.

SignupKit is the official framework by UVA Advancement Communications for enrolling users in email publications sent through the constituent management system, iModules. The included RESTful API transmits data via a proxy to a public API (SignupCore) maintained by Advancement Communications.

When transmitting an entry, SignupKit sends data to SignupCore as a JSON Web Token through a proxy file on the installation's server. Each installation is assigned a unique shared secret used to encrypt the transmitted data, which SignupCore then decrypts.

Securely processed and stored data for $50M+ in transactions

Jordan proved a quick study at mastering all existing applications and frameworks used to provide services to our wide range of stakeholders. He proposed new methods for using APIs to integrate disparate platforms to provide content and track user data and financial transaction history. He wrote the necessary code and set up a caching system to leverage this integration, <mark>bringing a new level of sophistication to our websites that provides meaningful content to viewers in real time.</mark>

The iModules Caching System powered the University of Virginia's central giving websites. It securely collected and encrypted gifts made to the University through the iModules donation platform, then served real-time gift information through a series of RESTful APIs to some of our most compelling sites. In all, it stored information for over $50 million in transactions.

Every five minutes, the system worked out the right date and time parameters from its previous successful calls. It requested donation data over SOAP, received it as XML, de-duplicated it, assigned unique IDs, and encrypted and stored the values.

Developers could also extend it. A set of predefined hooks let them add their own functionality during the caching process, and at the University of Virginia we used those hooks to make additional calls to the iModules API and to email UVA fundraisers through Amazon Web Services' Simple Email Service.
The caching system that securely stored fundraising data for UVA's giving sites.

At the heart of the University of Virginia's central giving sites was Alderman, a customizable parent theme. Alderman gave editors an adaptable admin interface and a core set of modular UI elements to build pages from, which drastically cut the turnaround time for new pages and still left room for creative freedom.

On the technical side, the theme grew out of the site's evolution and followed best practices for dependency management and performance optimization. Because the modular elements lived in one core theme, changing or adding a feature meant doing it once. Shortcodes made it quick to drop SVG animations, mobile-ready background videos, and additional stylesheets or scripts into a page.

The frontend of every site built on Alderman was built with Sass and jQuery, with Grunt compiling the Sass into CSS and building the JavaScript. The backend ran on PHP, and the APIs were built with Slim and Guzzle.
A modular WordPress parent theme that powered UVA's giving sites and cut page turnaround time.
